newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's two biggest rail unions set Jan 30 strike.
newsitem.headline: France's two biggest rail unions set Jan 30 strike.

text.p: France's two biggest rail unions called on Wednesday for a strike on January 30 against government plans to reform the heavily-indebted SNCF state railways being debated in the Senate.

The Communist-led CGT and the Socialist-led CFDT, which between them represent a majority of the 180,000 rail workers, said after a meeting that they had agreed on "a united reaction by rail workers to oppose the breakup of the SNCF".
The centre-right government's plan calls for the SNCF to be split with a new state company, likely to be called France Rail, owning the railtrack and most of the SNCF's debts.

The CFDT urged workers to hold mass meetings to set protest actions, "in the spirit of November and December 1995", when a 24-day rail strike paralysed France, forcing the government to withdraw a previous plan to streamline the railways.
The small SUD-Rail union, which staged an ineffecutal strike on Tuesday, said it would join the January 30 action.
However other rail unions are ready to back the latest reform plan, under which the railtrack company would take over 134.2 billion francs ($24.87 billion) of SNCF debts totalling 208 billion.

SNCF chairman Louis Gallois says the overhaul, which involves a measure of regionalisation, will benefit travellers who in some cases would see cheaper fares, while rail staff will not lose their benefits.
However militant unions fear an eventual breakup of the state rail monopoly, under European Union pressure, to let in private or foreign competition.
They are also determined to preserve their civil servant status and early retirement rights, which the government failed to alter in 1995 and has now agreed to leave alone.

The government, which insists the reform does not amount to a breakup, postponed the reform last November in the face of union disquiet and increased the amount of debt it was prepared to take off SNCF's shoulders by nearly 10 billion francs.
